progressionInfo.name: I-V-♭VII-IV Rock Anthem
progressionInfo.subtitle: The anthem-building progression that combines the triumphant pull of the V chord with the rebellious edge of the ♭VII borrowed from Mixolydian mode. This four-chord engine powers arena rock choruses, classic rock anthems, and singalong moments that demand fists in the air.

properties.label: I (Tonic)
properties.value: Establishes home base; the progression launches from and returns to this chord

properties.label: V (Dominant)
properties.value: Provides strong upward energy and forward momentum toward the ♭VII

properties.label: ♭VII (Subtonic)
properties.value: Borrowed from Mixolydian/parallel minor; adds a rock-modal edge that defies classical expectation

properties.label: IV (Subdominant)
properties.value: Provides warm plagal resolution back to the tonic, completing the anthem cycle

properties.label: Overall Motion
properties.value: Ascends from I to V, then descends through ♭VII to IV, creating a powerful arch-shaped harmonic contour

examples.label: ♭VII
examples.value: F Major (F-A-C) - borrowed from G Mixolydian

examples.label: Harmonic Contrast
examples.value: The V (D) contains F# while the ♭VII (F) contains F♮, creating a dramatic semitone shift between chords

chordDiagrams.title: I-V-♭VII-IV in G Major
chordDiagrams.description: Open position voicings in the key of G:
practiceNotes: The move from D to F is the defining moment: F# in the D chord drops to F♮ in the F chord
The F barre chord is the trickiest shape; practice transitioning from D to F repeatedly
Listen for the descending bass movement from D down through F to C
Strum with confidence and volume; this progression is built for power

chordDiagrams.title: I-V-♭VII-IV in C Major
chordDiagrams.description: Alternative key with familiar open chord shapes:
practiceNotes: The B♭ is borrowed from C Mixolydian (C-D-E-F-G-A-B♭)
B♭ barre chord at fret 1 requires solid barre technique; start slow
Try a B♭ power chord (x-1-3-3-x-x) as a simpler alternative
C to G is easy; use the G-to-B♭ transition as your main practice focus

advancedApplications.title: Rhythm & Voicing Variations
advancedApplications.description: Ways to shape the anthem sound:
items: Strum each chord for two beats with accented downstrokes for a driving anthem feel
Use eighth-note strumming with palm mute on the low strings and open strums on the high strings
Try arpeggiated picking through each chord for a ballad or intro section
Add suspended chords (Dsus4 to D, Csus4 to C) for extra melodic movement
Double the ♭VII chord duration for dramatic emphasis before resolving to IV

advancedApplications.title: Power Chord & Arena Rock Versions
items: G5-D5-F5-C5 with heavy distortion for arena rock power
Add octave doublings in the bass for a massive low-end foundation
Use palm-muted verses that explode into open-chord choruses
Layer clean arpeggios over a distorted power chord rhythm for two-guitar arrangements
Try a half-time feel on the ♭VII-IV section to create a breakdown moment

advancedApplications.title: Key Transpositions
items: A Major: A - E - G - D (all open chords, very guitar friendly)
C Major: C - G - B♭ - F (requires barre chords for B♭ and F)
D Major: D - A - C - G (comfortable open shapes throughout)
E Major: E - B - D - A (great for power chord rock with open low E)
G Major: G - D - F - C (the classic key for this progression)

examples.title: "Born to Run" - Bruce Springsteen
examples.description: The ultimate rock anthem uses this progression to build unstoppable momentum through the chorus
examples.detail: The V-to-♭VII shift mirrors the lyrical theme of breaking free from convention

examples.title: "The Final Countdown" - Europe
examples.description: The iconic synth riff and chorus ride this progression with arena-filling power
examples.detail: The ♭VII adds dramatic tension before the IV resolves triumphantly

examples.title: "Gloria" - Them (Van Morrison)
examples.description: Garage rock classic that hammers the I-V-♭VII-IV cycle with raw energy in E major
examples.detail: E-B-D-A creates an irresistible three-chord (plus tonic) engine for call-and-response vocals

examples.title: "All the Small Things" - Blink-182
examples.description: Pop-punk anthem that uses the progression's inherent sing-along quality
examples.detail: Fast tempo and power chords give the ♭VII a punk edge rather than classic rock grandeur

examples.title: "Should I Stay or Should I Go" - The Clash
examples.description: Punk-meets-rock-n-roll energy with strong ♭VII presence in the verse riff
examples.detail: The ♭VII creates the rebellious sound that defined the Clash's approach

examples.title: "Rock and Roll All Nite" - KISS
examples.description: The quintessential arena rock singalong built on powerful chord movement
examples.detail: Simple power chord voicings let the vocal melody and crowd participation take center stage

practiceCategories.title: Chord Transitions
items: Practice the G-D-F-C cycle slowly at 60 BPM, holding each chord for 4 beats
Isolate the D-to-F transition: this is the hardest shift with the barre chord
Use a metronome and gradually increase tempo from 60 to 120 BPM
Try the progression in A major (A-E-G-D) for all-open-chord ease
Practice the F-to-C transition separately, keeping your index finger anchored

practiceCategories.title: Anthem Rhythm Patterns
items: Use driving eighth-note downstrokes for maximum arena rock energy
Practice a down-down-up-up-down-up strumming pattern at 100 BPM
Try accenting beats 2 and 4 with harder strums for a backbeat feel
Experiment with two bars per chord for a half-time anthem feel
Add open-string hammer-ons between chord changes for connecting riffs

practiceCategories.title: Soloing & Improvisation
items: Use G Mixolydian (G-A-B-C-D-E-F) over the entire progression for a unified modal sound
Emphasize B over the G chord, F# over D, F♮ over the F chord, and E over C for chord-tone targeting
Try G major pentatonic and add the ♭7 (F) when the ♭VII chord arrives
Record a loop of the progression and practice building solos that peak over the V chord
Experiment with sliding between F and F# during the D-to-F chord change for bluesy color

notatedExercises.title: Exercise 1: Open Chord Anthem in G
notatedExercises.description: Strum the I-V-♭VII-IV progression with whole notes to internalize the harmonic movement:
practiceNotes: Hold each chord for a full bar (4 beats) before changing
Listen carefully for the F#-to-F♮ shift when moving from D major to F major
Focus on clean chord voicings with no buzzing strings
Once comfortable, try half notes (2 beats per chord, two chords per bar)

notatedExercises.title: Exercise 2: Driving Eighth-Note Rhythm
notatedExercises.description: Arena rock strumming pattern with accented downbeats:
practiceNotes: Use all downstrokes for maximum power and attack
Start at 90 BPM and work up to 130 BPM for authentic anthem tempo
Accent beat 1 of each chord change to mark the harmonic rhythm clearly
Add palm muting on beats 3 and 4 for dynamic contrast

notatedExercises.title: Exercise 3: Power Chord Rock Version
notatedExercises.description: Play G5-D5-F5-C5 with distortion for full arena rock energy:
practiceNotes: Use root-fifth power chord shapes on the 6th and 5th strings
G5 at fret 3, D5 at fret 5 (A string), F5 at fret 1, C5 at fret 3 (A string)
Keep your picking hand tight with palm muting between chord hits
Try adding a quick open-string chug between each chord change for rhythmic drive

sections.title: G Mixolydian over the Progression
items: G Mixolydian: G - A - B - C - D - E - F - G
The F♮ (instead of F#) is the defining note that makes the ♭VII chord diatonic
Over the V chord (D major), the F# from D's chord tones clashes with Mixolydian's F♮ - use D major arpeggio there
The Mixolydian scale unifies the I, ♭VII, and IV chords under one modal umbrella
This scale gives you the classic rock lead sound heard in countless anthem solos

sections.title: Pentatonic Approaches
items: G major pentatonic (G-A-B-D-E) works cleanly over the I and V chords
Add the ♭7 (F) to create a Mixolydian pentatonic hybrid (G-A-B-D-F)
G minor pentatonic (G-B♭-C-D-F) provides bluesy grit over the ♭VII and IV
Mixing major and minor pentatonic creates the classic rock lead vocabulary

sections.title: Why V and ♭VII Together?
items: The V chord (D major with F#) pulls strongly toward the tonic via its leading tone
The ♭VII (F major with F♮) immediately contradicts that pull, creating surprise and power
This F#-to-F♮ semitone drop is the emotional core of the progression
It combines the strength of dominant function with the rebellion of modal borrowing
This duality is why the progression sounds both triumphant and edgy

sections.title: Plagal Resolution (♭VII-IV-I)
items: After the dramatic V-to-♭VII shift, the IV chord provides warm resolution
IV to I is a plagal cadence, softer and more open than V-I authentic cadence
The ♭VII to IV movement (F to C in G major) is itself a V-I relationship in the key of the IV chord
This embedded resolution within the borrowed chord realm gives the progression its satisfying cyclic quality
